nhanes_dxa_bodyfat_men_1999_2004.label: US men: DXA percent body fat percentiles by age (NHANES 1999-2004, NCHS Vital Health Stat 11(250))

values.method: DXA, Hologic QDR 4500A fan-beam, Discovery software v12.1

sources.title: Borrud LG, Flegal KM, Looker AC, Everhart JE, et al. Body composition data for individuals 8 years of age and older: U.S. population, 1999-2004. NCHS Vital Health Stat 11(250), 2010. Table 3 (PDF sha256 686bf1c5c0b3d4fb...)

nhanes_dxa_bodyfat_men_1999_2004.notes: Table 3, 'Total percentage body fat ... Male, All race and ethnicity': 'Age 20 years and older, crude ... 6,559 28.0 0.1 17.4 19.5 21.4 24.1 28.0 32.1 34.3 35.9 38.0'; '20-39 years ... 2,183 26.1 0.1 15.5 17.4 18.9 21.2 26.1 30.4 32.8 34.6 37.2'. Methods: people over 300 lb or taller than 6'5" were not scanned ('physical limitations of the DXA table'). Missing or invalid scans were multiply imputed. 'Participant lean mass was decreased by 5% and an equivalent kilogram weight added to the fat mass', because the QDR 4500A was shown to underestimate fat (Schoeller et al.). The published %fat therefore already includes that correction. Weighted, nationally representative. Best primary source for 'everyday men'. Kelly, Wilson & Heymsfield 2009 (PLoS ONE, PMC2737140) uses the same NHANES DXA data. I fetched it, but its percentiles are in supplementary LMS files, so I used the NCHS tables instead.

nhanes_dxa_bodyfat_men_2011_2018.label: US men aged 20-59: age-adjusted mean DXA body fat by race and ethnicity, NHANES 2011-18 (Liu et al. 2021, BMJ)

sources.title: Liu B, Du Y, Wu Y, Snetselaar LG, Wallace RB, Bao W. Trends in obesity and adiposity measures by race or ethnicity among adults in the United States 2011-18: population based study. BMJ 2021;372:n365, Table 3 (Europe PMC full text PMC7961695)

nhanes_dxa_bodyfat_men_2011_2018.notes: Table 3 'Trends in age adjusted mean body fat percentage ... (n=10 864)', Men: Hispanic 27.8, 28.0, 28.4, 28.6; Non-Hispanic white 27.1, 27.9, 26.8, 27.2; Non-Hispanic black 25.0, 25.0, 24.9, 25.5; Non-Hispanic Asian 25.5, 26.7, 26.8, 28.2. 'Body fat percentage was available among adults aged 20-59 years.' Overall body fat was stable over 2011-18. The paper also says values were 'much higher' than 1999-2004. The DXA-ineligible share was small (0.1%). Table 3 has no all-race men figure, and I did not fetch the appendix. This confirms that the 1999-2004 NCHS percentiles are not out of date for men (about 25-29% means).

taylor2024_army_dxa_bodyfat.label: US Army active-duty men: DXA body fat in a representative sample (Taylor et al. 2024, USARIEM)

sources.title: Taylor KM, Castellani MP, Bartlett PM, Oliver TE, McClung HL. Development and cross-validation of a circumference-based predictive equation to estimate body fat in an active population. Obes Sci Pract 2024;10(2):e747, Tables 1-4 (Europe PMC full text PMC11026907)

taylor2024_army_dxa_bodyfat.notes: Abstract: 'Body size and composition were evaluated in a representatively sampled cohort of 1904 active-duty Soldiers (1261 Males, 643 Females), using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry'. Table 1, Men, Cohort 1: '% Body fatDXA 24.3 ± 6.3'; '% Body fatCIRC 19.5 ± 6.3' (the old AR 600-9 tape equation). Sampling was 'similar to those utilized in NHANES', with minorities oversampled. Cadets were excluded. The tabled FFM of 61.7 kg plus 21.5 kg fat is 83.2 kg, against a mean weight of 85.9 kg, so the 'fat-free mass' column probably excludes bone mineral (about 3 kg); treat it with care. Table 2 lists the male one-site manual equation (no height) as intercept -27.05, abdomen 2.06, weight -0.12, in inches and pounds judging by its closeness to the official equation. In the RMSE and bias tables the female column comes before the male one, which I inferred: the second column's old-AR bias of -4.79 matches the men's Table 1 difference of 19.5 - 24.3 = -4.8. This is the best measured body-fat value for US soldiers.

army_one_site_tape_equation_2023.label: US Army one-site (navel waist) body-fat equation, Army Directive 2023-11 (as published in an official Army installation summary)

sources.title: US Army Training Center & Fort Jackson Inspector General, 'IG Update 23-4: Guidance on Changes to Army Directive 2023-11 (Army Body Fat Assessment for the Army Body Composition Program)', FY23 Q4 (PDF sha256 236b7ad9...)
Army.mil, 'Evolving body composition standards in the U.S. Army: a science-informed approach' (background; 2021 USARIEM study of 2,690 soldiers)

army_one_site_tape_equation_2023.notes: The PDF reads: 'The equation for men is: % body fat = -26.97 - (0.12 x body weight in pounds) + (1.99 x abdomen circumference in inches)', with the worked example 'Abdomen = 35 inches; Weight = 210 pounds ... = -52.17 + 69.65 = 17 % (actual number is 17.48%...)'. It also says 'Beginning 8 June 2024, one-site tape test method is the only authorized method.' I did not fetch AD 2023-11 itself. This is an official Army installation summary of it. The Army.mil article says the change came from a 2021 USARIEM study of 2,690 soldiers compared against DXA. Taylor 2024 (separate key) gives a nearly identical one-site equation with an RMSE of about 3.4 percentage points in men.

ansur2_men_bodyfat_from_army_equation.label: ANSUR II men (n = 4,082): body fat estimated with the Army one-site equation from measured navel waist and weight, with the resulting FFMI and height-independent score

values.inputs: weightkg/10 -> lb; waistcircumference (mm, at omphalion) -> in; stature mm

sources.title: ANSUR II male public working database (repo copy, build-calculator/data/ansur2/ANSUR_II_MALE_Public.csv; provenance in existing key ansur2_dataset)
Fort Jackson IG Update 23-4 (AD 2023-11 one-site equation)
Taylor et al. 2024 Obes Sci Pract (PMC11026907)

ansur2_men_bodyfat_from_army_equation.notes: ANSUR II has no body-composition data (existing builds say 'unknown'). I computed these with the official equation, using ANSUR II's navel-level waist (same site as the Army abdomen tape) and scale weight. Script: scratchpad research/bodyfat/scripts/ansur_bf.py. Check: the equation's ANSUR II mean (24.1%) matches the measured DXA mean of 2021-22 soldiers (24.3%, Taylor 2024), though the equation was fitted to soldiers, so this is consistency, not proof. Taylor's own one-site coefficients give about 2.5 points more (mean 26.6%), so the method is uncertain by about that much. Individual error is about 3.4-4 points RMSE. The regression narrows the spread a little (predicted SD 5.7 vs measured 6.3). ANSUR II was measured in 2010-12 and the equation was fitted to 2021-22 soldiers. For the chart, the median ANSUR II man scores S ≈ 21 at these body fats. The brief's rough 'Army median about 24' implies about 15% fat, which is lower than measured soldiers.

barakat2022_natural_pro_peak_week_dxa.label: Barakat et al. 2022: self-described professional natural bodybuilder, DXA each day of peak week to competition morning

values.height: measured but not found in the text I parsed (unknown)

sources.title: Barakat C, Escalante G, Stevenson SW, Bradshaw JT, Barsuhn A, Tinsley GM, Walters J. Can Bodybuilding Peak Week Manipulations Favorably Affect Muscle Size, Subcutaneous Thickness, and Related Body Composition Variables? A Case Study. Sports 2022;10(7):106, Table 2 (Europe PMC full text PMC9321665)

barakat2022_natural_pro_peak_week_dxa.notes: Table 2 'Body Composition', DEXA: 'Competition Day | 73.55 | 6.3 | 4.63 | 68.91 | 2.591 | 66.32 | 3.6'. The subject is the first author: 'a Middle Eastern-American (29 years old ...) professional natural bodybuilder'. He placed first in Open Middleweight Bodybuilding and Classic Physique A (October 2021). Drug-free status is self-described, and the text I read does not say whether the show was tested. Daily DXA %fat moved by up to 0.9 points within 8 days as glycogen and water changed, which shows DXA noise at stage leanness. Ultrasound skinfolds (JP-7) read about 2-3 points lower than DXA.

kistler2014_natural_bb_dxa.label: Kistler et al. 2014: natural bodybuilder, 26-week prep for a pro-qualifier, DXA monthly

sources.title: Kistler BM, Fitschen PJ, Ranadive SM, Fernhall B, Wilund KR. Case study: Natural bodybuilding contest preparation. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab 2014;24(6):694-700 (PMID 24901578, abstract)

kistler2014_natural_bb_dxa.notes: Abstract: 'body composition was measured monthly by DXA ... Body weight (88.6 to 73.3 Kg ...) and percent body fat (17.5 to 7.4%) were reduced during preparation.' The 7.4% is the last monthly scan of prep, not necessarily contest day. The 17.5% start value is a useful natural off-season figure. Abstract only; height not given.

schoenfeld2020_natural_bb_case.label: Schoenfeld et al. 2020: high-level amateur natural bodybuilder over 4 competitions, about 5% fat just before competing

values.methods: multifrequency BIA and skinfolds (the abstract does not say which gave ~5%)

sources.title: Schoenfeld BJ, Alto A, Grgic J, et al. Alterations in body composition, resting metabolic rate, muscular strength, and eating behavior in response to natural bodybuilding competition preparation: a case study. J Strength Cond Res 2020;34(11):3124-3138 (PMID 33105363, abstract)

schoenfeld2020_natural_bb_case.notes: Abstract: 'Body fat was reduced to very low levels (~5%) immediately before competition, but this corresponded with a loss of lean mass.' A 'high-level amateur natural male bodybuilder'. Field methods (BIA, skinfolds) tend to read low at this leanness. Abstract only.

robinson2015_natural_bb_skinfold.label: Robinson et al. 2015: 21-year-old natural amateur bodybuilder, 14-week prep, skinfolds

sources.title: Robinson SL, Lambeth-Mansell A, Gillibrand G, Smith-Ryan A, Bannock L. A nutrition and conditioning intervention for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: case study. JISSN 2015;12:20, Table 2 and text (Europe PMC full text PMC4422265)

robinson2015_natural_bb_skinfold.notes: Table 2 baseline: 'Height (cm) 178.5; Body mass (kg) 86.0; Body fat (%) 14; Fat mass (kg) 11.7; Fat-free mass (kg) 74.3'. Text: 'a reduction of 6.7 kg's (or 6.8% body fat or 33 mm using sum of 8 skinfolds) and 5.0 kg's, in fat mass and FFM'. Body fat came from skinfolds with sex- and race-specific equations (ISAK protocol). End %fat (about 7.2%) and the FFMIs are my derivations. Skinfold method, lower quality than DXA or 4C.

mitchell2018_bodyfat_pct_derived.label: Mitchell et al. 2018: percent fat of 9 natural bodybuilders derived from their DXA fat and lean masses (relies on existing key mitchell2018_natural_bodybuilders)

sources.title: Mitchell L et al. Physiological implications of preparing for a natural male bodybuilding competition. Eur J Sport Sci 2018;18(5):619-629 (PMID 29490578, abstract)

mitchell2018_bodyfat_pct_derived.notes: Abstract: 'Fat mass (FM) was significantly reduced from PRE16 to PRE1 (8.8 ± 3.1 vs. 5.3 ± 2.4 kg ...). There was a small decrease in lean mass (LM) from PRE8 to PRE1 (71.8 ± 9.1 vs. 70.9 ± 9.1 kg'. Total mass and BMC are not in the abstract, so %fat is approximate. Fat over fat plus lean is an upper bound; adding an assumed 3.5 kg of bone mineral gives the lower figure. Ratio of group means, not mean of ratios. Result: about 7% one week out and about 10-11% 16 weeks out.

rosaci2026_ifbb_pro_case.label: Rosaci, Biban & Bartolomei 2026: IFBB Pro League ('Mr. Olympia competitor') bodybuilder, off-season and 10 days pre-contest, skinfold body fat

values.method: 3-site skinfold, Evans et al. 2005 athlete equation (4C-derived)

sources.title: Rosaci G, Biban S, Bartolomei S. Beyond the Limits of Human Muscle Hypertrophy: A Case Study of a Mr. Olympia Competitor Bodybuilder. J Strength Cond Res 2026;40(10):1253-1258, Table 3 and methods (Europe PMC full text PMC13592830)

rosaci2026_ifbb_pro_case.notes: Table 3: 'Body mass (kg) 128.7 | 122.3 ... % Body fat (%) 6.1 | 5.9; Fat-free mass (kg) 120.8 | 115.1' (BP = bulking/off-season, CT = cutting). Cutting measurement: 'June 11th, 2025 ... 10 days before the 2025 IFBB Huanji China Pro League competition'. Drug status: 'The eventual use of performance enhancing drugs by the athlete, competing in IFBB Pro League contests, in which antidoping tests are not performed, was not considered'. Equation: '% body fat = 8.997 + 0.24658 x (SUM 3 SKF) - 6.343 x (sex) - 1.998 x (race)'. For a white man it cannot go below 2.65% even at zero skinfold. A 6.1% off-season reading at 128.7 kg is implausibly low for this method and probably an underestimate. I treat the FFM, and so the FFMI of about 37-39, as upper bounds. Single subject. Best published body composition of a current top-level (presumably enhanced) pro that I found. The authors also cite Moreno et al. 2024 (Am J Hum Biol, PMID 37563889) for an Open bodybuilder of 131.4 kg at 12.2% fat. I fetched only Moreno's abstract, which gives ultrasound-estimated skeletal muscle (60.4 kg at most) and neither number, so the 12.2% is second-hand.

giakoni2025_mr_universe_bia.label: Giakoni-Ramirez et al. 2025: 18 male bodybuilders measured at the IFBB Mr. Universe (Santiago, Chile) after official weigh-in, BIA

sources.title: Giakoni-Ramirez F, Munoz-Strale C, de Souza-Lima J, et al. Hydration Strategies and Body Composition Differences in Male and Female Elite Bodybuilders During Competition. Nutrients 2025;17(9):1554, Table 2 (Europe PMC full text PMC12073694)

giakoni2025_mr_universe_bia.notes: Table 2, Males (n = 18): 'Weight (kg) 78.0 6.5; Height (cm) 171.3 3.7; Fat Mass (%) 8.9 1.8; Fat Free Mass (kg) 70.8 5.8'. Measured 'during the Mr. Universe Championship held in Santiago, Chile' after athletes had 'successfully passed the official weigh-in'. This is an IFBB amateur event. Drug status and testing are not stated. Hand-to-foot BIA in dehydrated, glycogen-loaded, very lean athletes is not reliable (see Raymond 2018: multifrequency BIA underestimated DXA %fat by 3.0 ± 3.8 points in football players). Use as a soft upper reference for stage leanness.

baggish2017_aas_users_ffmi.label: Baggish et al. 2017 (Pope group): normalized FFMI of 86 long-term AAS-using weightlifters vs 54 non-using weightlifters

sources.title: Baggish AL, Weiner RB, Kanayama G, Hudson JI, Lu MT, Hoffmann U, Pope HG. Cardiovascular Toxicity of Illicit Anabolic-Androgenic Steroid Use. Circulation 2017;135(21):1991-2002, Table 1 (NCBI PMC XML, PMC5614517)

baggish2017_aas_users_ffmi.notes: Table 1 (medians, IQR): 'Body mass index 31 (29-33) 29 (27-31); Fat-free mass index 26 (24-28) 23 (21-25)'. Footnote: 'The fat-free mass index is calculated as: (W(1-BF)/H^2) + 6.1(1.8-H)', so it is height-normalized with the 6.1 constant (see existing key ffmi_height_correction). Users had at least 2 years of cumulative AAS use; drug-test and hair-test screening was used. I did not find the body-fat method in the fetched text; the group has used skinfolds before, but that is not confirmed here. Medians, not maxima: a quarter of long-term users are below FFMI 24, so many enhanced lifters are not visibly beyond natural levels. Exclusion rule from the same paper: 'We also excluded men denying AAS use, but exhibiting a fat-free mass index greater than 26 kg/m2 together with body fat below 10%'.

hudson2020_aas_users_ffmi.label: Hudson et al. 2020 (Pope group, same cohort): normalized FFMI of current vs past AAS users vs non-users

sources.title: Hudson JI, Kanayama G, Pope HG, et al. Glomerular Filtration Rate and Supraphysiologic-Dose Anabolic-Androgenic Steroid Use: A Cross-sectional Cohort Study. Am J Kidney Dis 2020;76(2):296-299, Table 1 (NCBI PMC XML, PMC7744117)

hudson2020_aas_users_ffmi.notes: Table 1: 'Fat-free mass index 26 (24-28) 27 (25-29) 24 (25-28) 23 (21-25)' for all users (N = 85), current (N = 57), former (N = 28) and non-users (N = 52). The past-user cell '24 (25-28)' has a median outside its IQR, a typo in the source, so do not use it. Same FFMI formula (6.1 normalization). Current users' middle half spans 25-29, which overlaps the natural tail (Trexler 2017 football P97.5 = 28.1, existing key ffmi_athletes).

bulut2024_aas_users_lean_mass_index.label: Bulut et al. 2024 (Copenhagen): lean mass index and body fat in current and former AAS users vs strength-training controls

sources.title: Bulut Y, Rasmussen JJ, Brandt-Jacobsen N, et al. Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction Years After Cessation of Anabolic Androgenic Steroid Use. JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(12):e2451013, Table 1 (Europe PMC full text PMC11650407)

bulut2024_aas_users_lean_mass_index.notes: Table 1: 'Lean mass index, mean (SD), kg/m2 20 (2) 23 (2) 21 (2)'; 'Body fat, mean (SD), % 22 (4) 19 (3) 24 (4)'. Text: 'Individuals with current use (mean [SD], 19% [3%]) demonstrated lower body fat compared with controls (22% [4%])'. Men in recreational strength training, AAS status self-reported, with blinded urine analysis (Cologne). The main text does not name the body-composition method. The same group used DXA in Rasmussen 2017 (PMID 28500659), but I could not confirm DXA for this paper. 'Lean mass index' is probably lean soft tissue over height squared, excluding bone, so it reads about 1 below FFMI. Rounded to whole numbers in the source.

buhl2025_aas_users_bia.label: Buhl et al. 2025 (Denmark): body fat and BMI of current, previous and non-using male gym-goers, BIA

sources.title: Buhl LF, Christensen LL, Hjortebjerg R, et al. Illicit Anabolic Steroid Use and Cardiovascular Status in Men and Women. JAMA Netw Open 2025;8(8):e2526636, Table 1 (Europe PMC full text PMC12397887)

buhl2025_aas_users_bia.notes: Table 1, Men: 'Body fat percentage ... 13.1 (10.4-16.5) | 17.8 (12.3-21.2) | 20.0 (16.3-22.5)' (current, previous, non-users, median (IQR)); 'BMI ... 29.4 (27.7-32.2) ...'. Methods: 'body composition by bioimpedance (SOZO Digital Health Platform)'. Recruited from fitness centres March-December 2022. The current-user count of about 61 is inferred from a percentage row (15 = 24.6%). The FFMI of about 25.5 is a rough derivation from medians (29.4 x (1 - 0.131)), not a measured median. These are community users, not competitive bodybuilders.

bhasin_testosterone_ffm_gains.label: Bhasin et al. 1996 and 2001: fat-free mass gained on supraphysiologic testosterone (randomized trials)

bhasin2001.design: GnRH agonist + testosterone enanthate; no training
bhasin2001.ffm_method: DXA (per full paper; abstract says fat-free mass)

sources.title: Bhasin S, Storer TW, Berman N, et al. The effects of supraphysiologic doses of testosterone on muscle size and strength in normal men. N Engl J Med 1996;335(1):1-7 (PMID 8637535, abstract)
Bhasin S, Woodhouse L, Casaburi R, et al. Testosterone dose-response relationships in healthy young men. Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab 2001;281(6):E1172-81 (PMID 11701431, abstract)

bhasin_testosterone_ffm_gains.notes: 1996 abstract: 'The men received injections of 600 mg of testosterone enanthate or placebo weekly for 10 weeks ... fat-free mass was determined by underwater weighing ... The men assigned to testosterone and exercise had greater increases in fat-free mass (6.1 +/- 0.6 kg)'. 2001 abstract: 'Fat-free mass increased dose dependently in men receiving 125, 300, or 600 mg of testosterone weekly (change +3.4, 5.2, and 7.9 kg, respectively)'. I did not fetch the 2001 full text, so 'DXA' for that FFM is from memory of the paper and should be confirmed or dropped. These are short trials in men new to drugs; they show the size of early gains, not the long-term ceiling. The +2.4 FFMI is my conversion of 7.9 kg at 1.80 m.

nandrolone_bodybuilders_trials.label: Hartgens 2001 / van Marken Lichtenbelt 2004: 8 weeks of nandrolone decanoate 200 mg/week in experienced bodybuilders (randomized, placebo-controlled)

sources.title: van Marken Lichtenbelt WD, Hartgens F, Vollaard NB, Ebbing S, Kuipers H. Bodybuilders' body composition: effect of nandrolone decanoate. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2004;36(3):484-489 (PMID 15076791, abstract)

Hartgens F, van Marken Lichtenbelt WD, Ebbing S, et al. Body composition and anthropometry in bodybuilders: regional changes due to nandrolone decanoate administration. Int J Sports Med 2001;22(3):235-241 (PMID 11354529, abstract)

nandrolone_bodybuilders_trials.notes: 2004 abstract: '16 experienced male bodybuilders ... received ND (200 mg.wk-1 ...) or placebo for 8 wk. Body composition was assessed using the four-component model ... ND administration resulted in significant increments of body mass (+2.2 kg), fat-free mass (FFM: +2.6 kg)'. 2001 abstract (DXA): 'bone-free lean mass (from 59.54 +/- 2.36 to 63.06 +/- 2.99 kg ...)'. 'Total fat mass and total percentage fat remained unaffected'. The 200 mg/week dose is low compared with real use (see kaufman2024_aas_doses).

kaufman2024_aas_doses.label: Kaufman et al. 2024 (Pope group): self-reported AAS doses of long-term users

sources.title: Kaufman MJ, Hudson JI, Kanayama G, et al. A study of long-term supraphysiologic-dose anabolic-androgenic steroid use on cognitive function in middle-aged men. Am J Drug Alcohol Abuse 2024 (NCBI PMC XML, PMC11974399)

kaufman2024_aas_doses.notes: Table 1 (mean (SD)): 'Average weekly AAS dose, mg 973 (627); Maximum weekly AAS dose, mg 1978 (2130); Cumulative lifetime AAS use, yrs 10.0 (6.0)'. Self-reported. The same paper excluded a claimed non-user who 'displayed a fat-free mass index of 27.7 kg/m2 with a body fat of 7.5% - figures not plausibly attainable without use of performance-enhancing drugs'. That is the group's working natural boundary. Table 1 gives no FFMI.

yu2014_doped_vs_clean_powerlifters.label: Yu et al. 2014: lean body mass of long-term AAS-using vs clean strength athletes

sources.title: Yu JG, Bonnerud P, Eriksson A, Stal PS, Tegner Y, Malm C. Effects of long term supplementation of anabolic androgen steroids on human skeletal muscle. PLoS One 2014;9(9):e105330, Table 2 (Europe PMC full text PMC4160183)

yu2014_doped_vs_clean_powerlifters.notes: Table 2: 'Body weight (kg) 108±17 | 110±13; Lean body mass (kg) 89.8±8.2 | 74.6±6.8 (p = 0.06)'. Doping status was self-reported at interview. Same body weight, about 15 kg more lean mass in users, so users carried much less fat. Without heights no FFMI can be computed. Small sample. I did not confirm the scan method in the text I parsed.

kondo1994_sumo_ffm_limit.label: Kondo et al. 1994: professional sumo wrestlers, hydrodensitometry; largest FFM 121.3 kg

sources.title: Kondo M, Abe T, Ikegawa S, Kawakami Y, Fukunaga T. Upper limit of fat-free mass in humans: A study on Japanese Sumo wrestlers. Am J Hum Biol 1994;6(5):613-618 (PMID 28548340, abstract)

kondo1994_sumo_ffm_limit.notes: Abstract: 'Mean % fat of Sumo wrestlers, bodybuilders, and untrained subjects were, respectively, 26.1%, 10.9%, and 12.1% ... the largest one of 121.3 kg (stature: 186 cm, mass: 181 kg, %fat: 33.0%) ... It is suggested that a FFM/stature ratio of 0.7 kg/cm may be an upper limit in humans.' Two-compartment densitometry assumes a fixed FFM density, which is less accurate in very large or very muscular men (see existing key ffm_density_variation). Drug status of the 14 bodybuilders is not stated. Derived FFMI and S are mine. Abstract only.

hattori1999_sumo_divisions.label: Hattori et al. 1999: 36 professional sumo wrestlers, densitometry; FFMI about 30 separates top-division (sekitori) wrestlers

sources.title: Hattori K, Kondo M, Abe T, Tanaka S, Fukunaga T. Hierarchical differences in body composition of professional Sumo wrestlers. Ann Hum Biol 1999;26(2):179-184 (PMID 10195655, abstract)

hattori1999_sumo_divisions.notes: Abstract: 'The means of body weight, BMI and %fat for Sumo wrestlers were 117.1 kg, 36.5 and 26.2% ... The cut-off point of fat-free mass index which divided Sekitori wrestlers from other wrestlers is approximately 30'. The mean FFMI of 26.9 is my rough figure from group means (also listed in Martinez-Mireles 2025). Sumo wrestlers are not on the brief's group list, but they are the best-measured very heavy athletes and a useful 'strong and fat' reference.

bosch2019_d1_football_linemen_dxa.label: Bosch et al. 2019: DXA body composition by position, 467 NCAA Division I football players (C-CAR)

values.method: DXA, GE Lunar iDXA/Prodigy, central reanalysis enCore 16.2

sources.title: Bosch TA, Carbuhn AF, Stanforth PR, Oliver JM, Keller KA, Dengel DR. Body Composition and Bone Mineral Density of Division 1 Collegiate Football Players: A Consortium of College Athlete Research Study. J Strength Cond Res 2019;33(5):1339-1346, Tables 1-4 (NCBI PMC XML, PMC5591058)

bosch2019_d1_football_linemen_dxa.notes: 'Positional Body Composition Characteristics': 'Percent Fat (%) | 30.8a (4.2) | 23.5b (7.0) ...' for OL (n = 83) and DL (n = 53). Ranges table: OL 19-41%, DL 12-37%. 'All players were scanned on GE Healthcare Lunar systems'. Preseason (June-August) scans. 'Lean mass' excludes bone mineral, so lean-only FFMI reads about 1 low. NFL professionals by DXA appear only in a secondary review (martinezmireles2025_review_strength_sports): OL 28.8%, DL 25.2%. The NFL primary (Dengel et al. 2014, PMID 24149760) abstract gives no position %fat. Drug status of college players is not verified.

martinezmireles2025_review_strength_spor.label: Martinez-Mireles et al. 2025 scoping review: tabulated body fat of NFL linemen and heavyweight powerlifters (secondary)

NFL_OL_DXA.primary: Anding & Oliver 2015, GSSI Sports Science Exchange (Spanish)

NZ_heavyweight_powerlifters_anthropometr.primary: Keogh et al. 2007 (review mislabels as weightlifting)

sources.title: Martinez-Mireles X, et al. Defining Elite Zones: A Scoping Review of Body Physique and Body Fat in Elite Athletes. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 2025;11(1):13, table 'Body composition in elite male athletes with indirect methods' (Europe PMC full text PMC12821704)
Keogh JW, Hume PA, Pearson SN, Mellow P. Anthropometric dimensions of male powerlifters of varying body mass. J Sports Sci 2007;25(12):1365-76 (PMID 17786689, abstract)
Kraemer WJ et al. Body size and composition of National Football League players. J Strength Cond Res 2005;19(3):485-9 (PMID 16095394, abstract)

ffmi_definition_vanitallie1990.label: FFMI definition: fat-free mass over height squared (VanItallie et al. 1990)

sources.title: VanItallie TB, Yang MU, Heymsfield SB, Funk RC, Boileau RA. Height-normalized indices of the body's fat-free mass and fat mass: potentially useful indicators of nutritional status. Am J Clin Nutr 1990;52:953-959. doi:10.1093/ajcn/52.6.953 (Europe PMC abstract record, PMID 2239792)

ffmi_definition_vanitallie1990.notes: Abstract, verbatim: 'we propose use of height-normalized indices, namely, a FFM index [FFM (kg)/height (m)2, or FFMI] and a BFM index [BFM (kg)/height (m)2, or BFMI]. We calculated these indices in a reference population of 124 healthy young men and in 32 nonobese young men (from the Minnesota Study)'. The stated purpose is clinical: telling malnourished tall patients from well-nourished short ones. The abstract gives no reason for choosing height^2 over another power. The full text (OUP/Elsevier) was not reachable; only the abstract was read. Heymsfield 2007 later wrote that its results 'provide support for the suggestion of Van Itallie et al to normalize fat and FFM for height 2' (see heymsfield2007_ffm_height_power_fulltext). Existing builds.json key ffmi_definition_kouri_limit already has FFMI = FFM/H^2 from Kouri; this adds the original source.

geometric_similarity_mass_cubed.label: At the same shape and density, mass (and muscle mass) scales with height cubed and areas with height squared

Fowler M. Scaling: Why Giants Don't Exist. University of Virginia lecture notes (teaching source)

geometric_similarity_mass_cubed.notes:
Quotes:
- Burton 2010 abstract: 'As he [Quetelet] realised, perfect isometry or geometric similarity requires that body mass varies with height cubed'.
- Burton 2018 full text: 'consider first a hypothetical set of individuals of different sizes but identical density and bodily proportions. Their masses must vary in proportion to both (sitting height)3 and height3 ... The BMIs of these isometric individuals would inevitably increase with height.'
- Haldane: 'These monsters were not only ten times as high as Christian, but ten times as wide and ten times as thick, so that their total weight was a thousand times his, or about eighty to ninety tons. Unfortunately the cross sections of their bones were only a hundred times those of Christian'.
- Fowler: 'its height, length and breadth will all be doubled, so its volume -- and hence its weight -- will increase eightfold'; and 'a giant flea is one hundred times larger in all dimensions, so its weight is up by a factor of a million. Its amount of muscle is also up by a factor of a million'.
Evidence quality: this is geometry, not a measurement, so the statement is exact for a true scaled copy. Burton 2010 and 2018 are peer-reviewed. Haldane is a classic popular essay. The marxists.org transcription dates the essay 1928 (from the OUP 1985 collection), but the Harper's archive page metadata gives datePublished 1926-03-01. Fowler is university lecture notes. Schmidt-Nielsen 1984 (Cambridge UP) could not be read. The 60 ft = 18.3 m conversion is mine.

size_change_changes_form.label: Real bodies are not scaled copies across large size changes (Galileo, Haldane, McMahon, Biewener)

values.biewener2005_skeletal_scaling_mammals_bi: l proportional to d^0.89 (isometry d^1.0; elastic similarity d^0.67; stress similarity d^0.5)

sources.title: Galileo, Two New Sciences, First Day (Crew & de Salvio translation), reproduced by M. Fowler, University of Virginia
Haldane JBS. On Being the Right Size (marxists.org transcription)
McMahon T. Size and shape in biology. Science 1973;179:1201-1204 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 4689015)
Biewener AA. Biomechanical consequences of scaling. J Exp Biol 2005;208:1665-1676 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 15855398)

size_change_changes_form.notes:
Quotes:
- Galileo (Salviati): 'nature cannot produce a horse as large as twenty ordinary horses or a giant ten times taller than an ordinary man unless by miracle or by greatly altering the proportions of his limbs and especially of his bones'.
- Haldane: 'For every type of animal there is a most convenient size, and a large change in size inevitably carries with it a change of form.'
- McMahon abstract: elastic-stability arguments 'require that living organisms adopt forms whereby lengths increase as the (2/3) power of diameter'. It adds that Hill 'was forced to use an oversimplified "geometric similarity" hypothesis'.
- Biewener abstract: 'Although area:volume scaling predicts that stresses will increase with size, interspecific comparisons of mammals and birds show that skeletal allometry is modest, with most groups scaling (l ~ d^0.89) closer to geometric similarity (isometry: l ~ d^1.0) than to elastic similarity (l ~ d^0.67)'. It also says posture changes keep stresses fairly constant 'across a size range 0.04-300 kg. Above this size, extremely large mammals exhibit more pronounced skeletal allometry and reduced locomotor ability.'
Relevance: the height-cubed index measures shape (bulk for height) exactly. It says nothing about whether a 3 m, 2,700 kg body of that shape could carry itself. Rex and Ollie are indestructible by canon, so the page should say this and not imply real-world feasibility. Galileo's publication year is not on the fetched page.

rohrer_tri_ponderal_index.label: Rohrer / ponderal / tri-ponderal mass index: body mass over height cubed (kg/m^3)

sources.title: Peterson CM et al. Tri-Ponderal Mass Index vs Body Mass Index in Estimating Body Fat During Adolescence. JAMA Pediatr 2017;171:629-636 (PMC full text)
Peterson 2017 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 28505241)
Burton R. Children (Basel) 2018;5(2):30 (PMC full text; defines the Rohrer index)

Wikipedia: Corpulence index (wikitext; tertiary source, used only for the Rohrer 1921 citation)

rohrer_tri_ponderal_index.notes:
Quotes:
- Peterson 2017 full text: 'the tri-ponderal mass index (TMI = mass divided by height cubed [kilograms divided by meters cubed]), which is based on the ponderal index and the Rohrer Index (see eAppendix 1 in the Supplement for a historical overview)'.
- Peterson abstract: 'percent body fat scales to height with an exponent closer to 3'.
- Burton 2018: 'the Rohrer index, (body mass)/height 3'.
- Burton 2007 abstract: 'Mass/height(3) is an index of body build that is independent of scale and statistics.'
The Rohrer 1921 citation (Rohrer F. Der Index der Körperfülle als Maß des Ernährungszustandes. Münch Med Wochenschr 1921;68:580-582) comes only from Wikipedia. The primary was not fetched, and the Peterson supplement with the history was blocked by a PMC download challenge. Treat the year as reported, not verified. The name 'ponderal index' is also used for H / W^(1/3) (Wikipedia notes this), so the page should give the formula, not just the name.
These indices use total mass and were validated for fatness in children and adolescents, not for muscularity in adults. They are precedent for dividing by height cubed, not validation of a fat-free version.

ffm_over_height_cubed_literature.label: Published fat-free mass over height cubed index: none found; in children FFM is best adjusted by height squared

sources.title: Wells JC, Cole TJ, ALSPAC study team. Adjustment of fat-free mass and fat mass for height in children aged 8 y. Int J Obes 2002;26:947-952 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 12080448)

Ramírez-Vélez R et al. Tri-Ponderal Mass Index vs. Fat Mass/Height^3 as a Screening Tool for Metabolic Syndrome Prediction in Colombian Children and Young People. Nutrients 2018;10:412 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 29584641)

ffm_over_height_cubed_literature.notes:
Wells & Cole 2002 abstract: 'FFM was optimally adjusted for height by calculating FFM/HT(2). FM was optimally adjusted by calculating FM/HT(6).' The method used deuterium dilution, and the power p was chosen to remove the index's correlation with height. Ramírez-Vélez 2018 used 'fat mass (kg)/height (m³)', which is fat, not fat-free mass, and is a metabolic-syndrome screen.
Search done: Europe PMC abstract searches for 'fat-free mass' with 'height3' or 'height cubed', 'lean mass' with 'height cubed', 'FFM/height3' and 'lean mass index' with 'height3' returned 0 hits. 'fat-free mass' with 'height(3)' returned 6 hits, none defining an FFM/H^3 index.
Conclusion: 1.8 x FFM/H^3 is a derived construct of this project (the fat-free analogue of the Rohrer index, scaled to Kouri's 1.80 m). It must not be presented as a published index. The task brief's guess that Wells & Cole support a height-cubed FFM index is wrong: they found height squared for FFM.

heymsfield2007_ffm_height_power_fulltext.label: Adult FFM and skeletal muscle scale with height to a power of about 2, not 3 (Heymsfield 2007, full-text numbers)

sources.title: Heymsfield SB, Gallagher D, Mayer L, Beetsch J, Pietrobelli A. Scaling of human body composition to stature: new insights into body mass index. Am J Clin Nutr 2007;86:82-91 (PMC author manuscript, full text)
Same paper, Europe PMC abstract (PMID 17616766)

heymsfield2007_ffm_height_power_fulltext.notes:
Full text, verbatim:
- 'The similar compartment, FFM, scaled to height with respective powers of 1.86 ± 0.10 and 2.05 ± 0.09 in the NY-2 men and women. ... none of the β values differed significantly from 2.0.'
- 'Skeletal muscle mass scaled to height with powers of 1.98 ± 0.27 and 2.08 ± 0.20 in the NY-1 men and women'.
- Conclusions: 'weight, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, ATFM, and FFM all scale to height with powers of 2 as the nearest whole integer. These observations indicate that corresponding height-normalized indexes are also independent of height'.
Table 1: NY-1 has 178 men and 233 women (MRI plus DXA); NY-2 has 581 men and 765 women (DXA only).
This extends existing key heymsfield_2007_scaling, which has the abstract only, with the men's numbers. Caveats: general-population adults with BMI 18.5-35 and mean age about 45-50, not athletes; log-log least-squares regression (see height_exponent_regression_vs_isometry for why that may understate a structural exponent).
This is why plain FFMI is roughly height-independent among ordinary adults. FFM/H^1.86 vs FFM/H^2 differ by only (H/1.8)^0.14, under 2% across 1.65-1.95 m.

With allowance made for positive correlations with upper body mass, leg CSAs showed a negative correlation with leg length (P = 0.00006-0.027).' height_exponent_regression_vs_isometry.label: Is the human mass-height exponent really about 2, or nearer 3? (regression vs Burton's isometry hypothesis)

sources.title: Burton RF. Human allometry: adult bodies are more nearly geometrically similar than regression analysis has suggested. Med Hypotheses 2010;74:15-17 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 19726135)
Burton RF. Ann Hum Biol 2007;34:656-663 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 18092209)
Heymsfield 2007 full text (PMC2729090)

height_exponent_regression_vs_isometry.notes:
Burton 2010 abstract:
- 'Values of b estimated by regression must usually underestimate the true functional values, doing so especially when mass and height are poorly correlated.'
- Published b 'for the whole body (which range between 1.0 and 2.5)'.
- 'Monte Carlo modelling has shown that the results obtained for total body mass are compatible with a true height exponent of three.'
Burton 2007 abstract: 'In adult populations mass must vary more nearly with height(3) than with height(2), although ... conventional statistical techniques suggest otherwise'.
Against this, Heymsfield 2007 finds FFM powers near 2 in large samples, and Burton 2012 (tall_men_not_scaled_copies) itself finds legs relatively thinner in long-legged people.
The ANSUR OLS (2.0) vs RMA (4.24) exponents come from existing key ansur_mass_height_exponent; that key already says neither should be used as the exponent for 'the same build at another height'. Burton 2010 is a Medical Hypotheses paper: argument plus modelling, no new measurements.
Status disputed: the structural exponent for real humans is unsettled. This matters only for how the index treats ordinary tall vs short men. It does not affect the exact statement that a true scaled copy has mass proportional to H^3.

allometric_normalisation_practice.label: Sport science normalises for body size with theoretical geometric-similarity exponents (allometric scaling)

sources.title: Jaric S, Mirkov D, Markovic G. Normalizing physical performance tests for body size: a proposal for standardization. J Strength Cond Res 2005;19:467-474 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 15903392)
Jaric S. Muscle strength testing: use of normalisation for body size. Sports Med 2002;32:615-631 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 12141882)
Nevill AM, Ramsbottom R, Williams C. Scaling physiological measurements for individuals of different body size. Eur J Appl Physiol 1992;65:110-117 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 1396632)

allometric_normalisation_practice.notes:
Jaric 2005 abstract: 'we propose (a) using an allometric normalization based on theoretical models that presume geometric similarity'. Jaric 2002 abstract: 'The allometric parameter should be either b = 0.67 for muscle force ... or b = 1 for muscle torque'. Nevill 1992 abstract: 'the best method of scaling maximum oxygen uptake, peak and mean power output, required these variables to be divided by body mass, recorded in the units kg 2/3'.
The exponent 0.67 = 2/3 is the geometric-similarity exponent (area over volume). That derivation is mine; the Jaric 2002 abstract does not spell it out.
Relevance: when bodies differ in size, the field's recommended practice is to divide by the size power implied by geometric similarity, not by a ratio picked for convenience. For mass against height that power is 3. These papers normalise performance, not body composition, and cover human ranges only.

rescaled_ffmi_identity_at_180.label: Rescaled FFMI S = 1.8 x FFM / H^3 equals plain FFMI at exactly 1.80 m

sources.title: Kouri 1995 abstract (reference height 1.80 m)
VanItallie 1990 abstract (FFMI definition)

rescaled_ffmi_identity_at_180.notes:
Algebra: at H = 1.8, S = 1.8 x FFM / 1.8^3 = FFM / 1.8^2 = FFMI. Script check: scratchpad/research/size_index/scripts/derived.py (the difference is floating-point rounding only).
Meaning: S is the plain FFMI the same body would have if all its lengths were scaled to 1.80 m, keeping its shape and density. At 1.80 m it also equals Kouri's normalised FFMI, since Kouri's correction is zero there. So Kouri's 25.0 non-user maximum (existing key kouri1995_ffmi_natural_limit) can be drawn on the S axis at 25 without conversion, as a line from a human sample, not a ceiling. Equivalently, S = 1.8 m x (fat-free Rohrer index in kg/m^3).

same_shape_scaled_to_3048.label: The same shape scaled from 1.80 m to 3.048 m: plain FFMI rises 1.69 times, the rescaled index does not change

sources.title: Burton 2018 (isometric individuals: mass proportional to height^3; BMI rises with height)
Burton 2010 (geometric similarity requires mass proportional to height cubed)

same_shape_scaled_to_3048.notes: k = 3.048 / 1.8 = 1.6933. A scaled copy has FFM multiplied by k^3 = 4.855, so plain FFMI = FFM/H^2 is multiplied by k^3 / k^2 = k = 1.693, while S = 1.8 x FFM/H^3 is multiplied by k^3 / k^3 = 1. The 269 plain FFMI for Rex at 7.5% fat (tail included, height to crest 3.048 m) comes from the brief, not recomputed here. 269 / 1.6933 = 158.9, matching the brief's 'about 159'. kouri_correction_beyond_human_heights.label: Kouri's linear height correction fails far outside human heights (Rex: 261 vs 159)

sources.title: Kouri 1995 abstract (correction 6.3 x (1.80 - height))

kouri_correction_beyond_human_heights.notes:
Arithmetic in scratchpad/research/size_index/scripts/derived.py.
- Kouri adds a fixed c x (1.80 - H). At 3.048 m that is -7.6 (c = 6.1) or -7.9 (c = 6.3), so Rex's plain 269 becomes about 261. The same-shape rescaling gives 159.
- For a same-shape body, FFMI(H) = S x H / 1.8, so near 1.80 m the exact same-shape correction has slope FFMI/1.8 per metre: 13.9 at FFMI 25.
- Kouri's 6.3 is about 45% of that slope at FFMI 25. This is equivalent to assuming FFM proportional to H^2.45 (agrees with existing key ffmi_height_correction).
- Because the correction is a constant slope, not a ratio, it cannot scale with the size of the body. It was fitted on human athletes only (height range not in the abstract; full text unavailable).
The Build Calculator's calc.js already applies Kouri only between 1.55 and 2.05 m (FFMI_NORM_RANGE) with c = 6.1. The chart should not use Kouri for comic characters beyond that range, nor for Rex or Ollie.

rescaled_vs_kouri_human_heights.label: Within human heights, the rescaled index and Kouri's normalised FFMI differ by up to about 2.5 units (at plain FFMI 25)

sources.title: Kouri 1995 abstract (correction formula)

rescaled_vs_kouri_human_heights.notes:
Computed for a man with plain FFMI 25 at each height (scripts/derived.py). Kouri values with c = 6.3 differ from c = 6.1 by 0.05 or less. Within 1.70-1.90 m the two agree within 0.9 units. At 1.55 m S is 2.5 units higher, and at 2.05 m it is 1.5 units lower.
The direction matches the ANSUR finding: S favours short men and penalises tall men relative to the human-fitted correction. This is because Kouri's correction implies FFM proportional to H^2.45 and S assumes H^3.
Example with existing builds: a 1.91 m strongman or a 1.73 m bodybuilder will sit about 1 unit apart on the two scales. Show both for human builds so readers can see the gap.

rescaled_index_height_sensitivity.label: The rescaled index falls with height cubed: each 1% of height is about 3% of score

sources.title: Burton 2010 (mass proportional to height cubed at the same shape)

rescaled_index_height_sensitivity.notes: S proportional to H^-3 at fixed FFM: 1/1.01^3 = 0.9706 and 1/0.99^3 = 1.0306. This is why the brief requires height to the top of the skull, not to Rex's crest or Ollie's horn tips. Example from existing key rex_ollie_picture_mass: Ollie is 3.063 m to his horn tips and 2.982 m to his skull top. That is a 2.7% height difference, so his S is 8.3% higher with the skull-top height ((3.063/2.982)^3 = 1.083). For real people, a 1 cm error in a reported height at 1.80 m (0.56%) moves S by about 1.7%.

meatball_score_check.label: Upper bound: a solid ball of tissue as tall as the figure scores about 924 at 7.5% fat (899-949 for 5-10%)

sources.title: Existing builds.json key rex_ollie_picture_mass (whole-body density 1,060 kg/m^3 = 1,081 x 0.98 lung gas)
Existing builds.json key muscle_tissue_density (Ward & Lieber 2005: conventional 1,059.7 kg/m^3)

meatball_score_check.notes:
A ball of diameter H has volume (pi/6) H^3, so FFM = rho x (pi/6) H^3 x (1 - f) and S = 1.8 x rho x (pi/6) x (1 - f), whatever H is. 1.8 x 1060 x 0.5236 x 0.925 = 924.1, matching the brief.
The 1,060 kg/m^3 is the whole-body density used for Rex and Ollie, including about 2% lung gas (existing key rex_ollie_picture_mass; I did not re-fetch its sources). With lung-free tissue at 1,081 kg/m^3, S would be about 942. Use the same density as the duo so the top of the scale and the duo stay comparable.
At 3.048 m the same ball has plain FFMI 1,565. That is the plain-FFMI ceiling the page must not mix with S. This is geometry with an assumed density, not a physiological limit.

recommended_size_independent_index.label: Recommendation: keep S = 1.8 x FFM / H^3 ('FFMI at 1.80 m, same shape'); no better-sourced alternative found

rejected.kouri_normalised: linear, fitted to human athletes; 261 vs 159 for Rex

values.known_bias_humans: tall men score lower: tallest ANSUR decile about 12% below shortest at equal BMI

sources.title: Burton 2007 (mass/height^3 independent of scale)
Burton 2018 full text (isometric individuals)
Jaric 2005 (allometric normalisation based on geometric similarity)
Kouri 1995 abstract (1.80 m reference)
Heymsfield 2007 full text (FFM ~ H^1.86 in men)

recommended_size_independent_index.notes:
Why this index:
- The height-cubed exponent is the only one that follows from geometry: constant for a scaled copy (Burton 2007, 2010, 2018; Haldane; Fowler).
- Allometric normalisation based on geometric similarity is the recommended practice when sizes differ (Jaric 2005).
- Weight/H^3 is an established index (Rohrer, tri-ponderal; Peterson 2017).
- The constant 1.8 m is Kouri's reference height, so S equals plain and Kouri-normalised FFMI at 1.80 m. That lets readers use the familiar FFMI landmarks (Schutz median 18.9, Kouri 25) on the S axis.
Where S stops being valid, or misleads:
1. Real tall men are not scaled copies. FFM goes roughly with H^1.86 to 2 (Heymsfield 2007), so S rates ordinary tall men lower and short men higher (ANSUR: about 12% between the tallest and shortest tenths). Kouri-normalised FFMI is the better human comparison between 1.55 and 2.05 m.
2. S is not a published FFM index (none found). Kouri's 25 is a sample maximum in normalised FFMI, which equals S only at 1.80 m. At other human heights the two differ by up to about 2.5 units.
3. S measures bulk for height (shape), not strength or physiology. It says nothing about whether a 3 m body of that shape could stand or move (Galileo, Haldane, Biewener).
4. S is very sensitive to the height used (3% per 1%) and to the assumed density and body fat.
5. Every S above the human data (about 40) is an extrapolation of geometry, not of any fitted human relation.

kouri1995_fulltext_methods.label: Kouri et al. 1995, full text: sample, how non-use was checked, body-fat method, group values, and the 6.1 height slope

sources.title: Kouri EM, Pope HG Jr, Katz DL, Oliva P. Fat-free mass index in users and nonusers of anabolic-androgenic steroids. Clin J Sport Med 1995;5(4):223-228. Publisher's free full-text PDF (Ovid / Wolters Kluwer; scanned, 6 pages; read as page images)
Same article, publisher landing page reached from DOI 10.1097/00042752-199510000-00003 (marked 'Free', 'PDF Only')
Europe PMC record, PMID 7496846 (abstract)

kouri1995_fulltext_methods.notes:
Methods, p.223: 'One hundred fifty-six men in a large controlled study of athletes, recruited at gymnasiums in the Boston and Los Angeles areas, were administered physical examinations ... height, body weight, and body fat, the latter computed from the sum of six skinfold measurements using an equation derived from the data of Jackson and Pollock'. The equation is %fat = 0.217x1 - 0.00029x1^2 + 0.133x2 - 5.73, where x1 is the sum of the chest, thigh, ilium, abdomen, triceps and scapula skinfolds and x2 is age. One investigator (H.G.P.) took all the skinfolds.

Non-use, p.223-224: 'Each athlete's history of steroid use was obtained by detailed personal interview, supplemented by urine testing ... no evidence suggested that any athlete had deliberately misrepresented his steroid use, nor did any urine test contradict an athlete's verbal report.' p.226: 'all 74 nonusers produced urine samples negative for steroids.' A urine test shows only recent use, so past use rests on the interview.

Sample, p.224: 'complete skinfold measurements were not performed in 22 subjects, leaving 134 evaluable individuals'. Added to them were 23 men from a testosterone cypionate trial: 'five men who had formerly used anabolic steroids and 18 who had not'. On the non-users: 'The nonusers included many dedicated bodybuilders. Several had competed successfully in "natural" bodybuilding contests, two held world records in strength events, and many others were recognized by their associates as highly successful weightlifters.'

Formulas: FFM = weight x [1 - (%fat / 100)]; FFMI = FFM x height^-2.

Table 1 (mean +/- SD; the FFMI here is before height normalisation):
- Users: 1.79 +/- 0.075 m, 91.69 +/- 11.8 kg, 12.8 +/- 4.8% fat, FFMI 24.8 +/- 2.2.
- Non-users: 1.80 +/- 0.074 m, 82.06 +/- 13.0 kg, 12.5 +/- 5.5% fat, FFMI 21.8 +/- 1.8.

Users vs non-users, p.224: 'users extended well beyond the line, with 37 (45%) of the users attaining levels of FFMI beyond the uppermost of the nonusers.'

Height slope, p.224: 'we calculated the slope of a regression line drawn through a plot of all the "elite" nonuser athletes with FFMI scores of 22 or above ... This calculation yielded a slope of 6.1 kg/m3 ... Normalized FFMI = FFMI + 6.1 x (1.8 - h)'. The 1.8 m is 'the mean height of the nonusers'. The abstract's '6.3' does not appear in the body of the paper.

Height effect: the paper re-measured 'the shortest nonuser (height 1.59 m) and one of the tallest nonusers (height 1.93 m)'. Their unnormalised FFMIs were 23.5 and 25.4, yet 'the short athlete appeared more muscular'.

Limitations the authors give:
- 74 non-users 'might not have been large enough to exhibit fully the upper limits of muscularity naturally attainable'.
- The skinfold standard error is 3.4% fat. Their example: a 1.8 m, 90 kg man at 10% fat scores 25.0, and at 13% fat 24.2.
- 'it is possible that fat individuals might be able to exceed substantially an FFMI of 25 without steroids'. Only 6 non-users (8.1%) were above 20% fat.

Small internal slip: 'Fifty-two of the users (67% of the user group)'. 52/83 is 63%; 52/78 gym-study users is 67%.

Evidence quality: one cross-sectional sample of self-selected volunteers with one skinfold tester. It is strong evidence that these 74 men stopped below 25, and weak evidence for any population-wide ceiling.

kouri1995_fig2_distribution.label: Kouri 1995 Fig. 2: every non-user's and user's normalised FFMI, in 1-unit bins (counted from the figure)

sources.title: Kouri et al. 1995, Clin J Sport Med 5:223-228, Fig. 2 (p.225), publisher's free PDF

kouri1995_fig2_distribution.notes:
Counted by script (scratchpad scripts/count_dots.py, page rendered at 250 dpi) from Fig. 2, captioned 'FFMI, normalized to the height of a 1.8-m man in 74 nonusers ... and 83 users ... Each circle represents one individual.'

Bin counts:
- Non-users, bins 17-17.9 to 24-24.9: 1, 5, 4, 16, 16, 13, 10, 9 (total 74).
- Users, bins 19-19.9 to 31-31.9: 1, 3, 6, 6, 16, 14, 15, 5, 9, 3, 3, 1, 1 (total 83).

The 37 users at or above 25 match the text's '37 (45%)'. Text p.224: 'the nonusers "stop" abruptly at a maximum value of 25.0'. p.226: 'athletes who had not used steroids all had values of <25.0'. So the top non-user lies between 24.0 and 24.9, with 9 men in that bin; the paper does not print the exact top value.

The highest user is in the 31.0-31.9 bin, and 2 users exceed 30. Helms' 'some users reached ~32' rounds up. 46 of the 83 users (55%) were below 25, so an FFMI under 25 is no evidence that a man is natural.

In Fig. 1 (unnormalised FFMI against height) the top user sits at about 31, near 1.73 m. That is read off the plot, so it is approximate.
